maths_eduqas_f.3.1.summary: Mastering ruler and compass constructions and loci is essential for precise geometrical drawing and problem solving in GCSE Mathematics. These revision notes cover the fundamental geometric constructions including perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors, perpendiculars from a point, and constructing triangles. Additionally, they explain how loci create regions of points satisfying given conditions, and why perpendicular distance represents the shortest distance from a point to a line.

core.h: Introduction to Ruler and Compass Constructions
core.p: In GCSE geometry, construction questions require the use of a sharp pencil, a ruler, and a pair of compasses. Freehand drawings will score zero marks, and compass arcs must always be left visible to prove the method used.
bullets: Never rub out construction arcs as examiners check them for method marks.
A ruler is used strictly for drawing straight lines, never for measuring lengths unless explicitly instructed.
Compasses must be tightened so the pencil does not slip while drawing arcs.
Always ensure your pencil is sharp for pinpoint accuracy.

callouts.p: Leaving construction arcs visible is compulsory for gaining full marks in exam construction questions.

core.h: Perpendicular Bisector of a Line Segment
core.p: A perpendicular bisector divides a line segment exactly in half at a 90-degree angle. It is also the locus of all points equidistant from the two endpoints of the line segment.
bullets: Place the compass point on endpoint A and open the compasses to more than half the length of AB.
Draw an arc above and below the line segment.
Keeping the exact same compass radius, place the compass point on endpoint B and draw arcs to intersect the previous two arcs.
Join the two intersection points with a straight line using a ruler.

callouts.p: A line that cuts another line segment at right angles (90 degrees) and divides it into two equal halves.
If your arcs do not intersect, your compass opening was less than half the length of the line segment.

fig.cap: Constructing the perpendicular bisector of line segment AB using intersecting compass arcs.

core.p: An angle bisector divides an angle into two equal smaller angles. It is also the locus of points equidistant from the two lines forming the angle.
bullets: Place the compass point on the vertex of the angle and draw an arc that cuts both arms of the angle.
Place the compass point where the arc crosses one arm and draw an arc inside the angle.
Keeping the same radius, place the compass point where the arc crosses the other arm and draw an arc to intersect the previous one.
Draw a straight line from the vertex through the intersection of the arcs.

callouts.p: The resulting two angles either side of the bisector line are identical in size.

core.h: Perpendicular from a Point to a Line
core.p: To drop a perpendicular line from a given point to a given line, or to construct a perpendicular at a point on a line, compasses are used to establish symmetric reference points.
bullets: If constructing from a point not on the line: place the compass on the point and draw an arc that cuts the line in two places.
Find the midpoint between these two intersection points on the line.
Join the original point to this midpoint using a straight line.
Ensure the angle formed is clearly a right angle.

callouts.p: Do not use a protractor to measure 90 degrees in construction questions; examiners require compass arcs.

core.p: Constructions are frequently used to draw triangles accurately when given specific side lengths or angles. SSS uses compasses for all sides, SAS uses a ruler and compass, and ASA uses a protractor or ruler.
bullets: For SSS (Side-Side-Side): draw the base with a ruler, set compasses to the second side length and arc from one end, then set compasses to the third side length and arc from the other end.
For SAS (Side-Angle-Side): draw the first side, measure the given angle accurately, draw the second side, and join the ends.
For ASA (Angle-Side-Angle): draw the base line, measure the angles at each end, and extend the lines until they intersect.
Label all vertices clearly with capital letters.

callouts.p: Double-check your compass measurements against your ruler before drawing arcs.

core.p: A locus (plural: loci) is a set of points that follow a specific rule or condition. Instead of just a single point or line, a locus often forms a region or a continuous path.
bullets: Locus of a point at a fixed distance from a point is a circle.
Locus of a point equidistant from two points is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them.
Locus of a point equidistant from two intersecting lines is the angle bisector.
Locus of a point at a fixed distance from a straight line is a pair of parallel lines with rounded ends.

callouts.p: A collection of points satisfying a given geometric condition or set of conditions.

core.h: Perpendicular Distance as the Shortest Distance
core.p: The shortest distance from a given point to a straight line is always measured along the perpendicular line drawn from the point to that line.
bullets: Any diagonal or slanted line from the point to the line will always be longer than the perpendicular drop.
In exam questions asking for the closest point on a boundary, construct a perpendicular line from the object to the boundary.
Use your ruler to measure this perpendicular distance according to the given scale.
This principle is fundamental in navigation, optimization, and region shading.

callouts.p: Perpendicular distance equals the shortest possible distance from a point to a line.

core.p: When a question asks for the locus of a point that stays a fixed distance, say 4 cm, from a fixed point P, the result is a circle with centre P and radius 4 cm.
bullets: Set your compasses to the required radius using a ruler.
Place the compass point on the fixed point P.
Draw a complete circle or the required arc segment.
Check the scale if a map or blueprint is used (e.g., 1 cm represents 2 km).

callouts.p: Always convert real-life distances to drawing measurements using the given scale before setting your compasses.

core.p: If a point must remain equidistant from two fixed points A and B, its locus is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment AB.
bullets: Draw a straight line connecting point A to point B.
Construct the perpendicular bisector of line AB.
Any point lying on this bisector is guaranteed to be the exact same distance from A as it is from B.
Shade or indicate the required side of the line if a region is requested.

callouts.p: Equidistant simply means 'equal distance'.

core.p: If a point must remain equidistant from two intersecting straight lines, its locus is the angle bisector(s) of the angle(s) formed by the lines.
bullets: Extend the lines if necessary so they intersect.
Construct the angle bisector between the two lines.
Remember that intersecting lines form four angles, so there may be two perpendicular intersecting angle bisectors.
Identify the correct quadrant or region specified in the exam question.

callouts.p: The locus of points equidistant from two straight lines is the angle bisector.

core.p: Exam questions often combine multiple loci conditions and ask you to shade the region that satisfies all conditions simultaneously.
bullets: Construct each locus accurately using construction lines and compasses.
Read inequality symbols carefully: '<' or '>' for dashed boundaries (though usually solid in GCSE unless specified), and 'less than' meaning inside an arc, 'greater than' meaning outside.
Shading the unwanted region makes it easier to see the final unshaded target region, or vice versa depending on exam board convention (always follow the specific instruction 'shade the region').
Label the final region clearly with the letter R if requested.

callouts.p: Always re-read the inequality carefully. 'Within 5 cm' means inside the circle; 'more than 5 cm' means outside.

core.p: Examiners penalise missing construction arcs and inaccurate measurements. Being methodical ensures full marks on high-tariff construction and loci questions.
bullets: Keep your pencil sharp so intersections are precise points, not thick blurry blobs.
Never rub out your compass construction lines.
Check whether your final answer requires a point, a line, or a shaded region.
Ensure your compasses do not slip during drawing.

callouts.p: Arcs visible? Yes. Ruler used for straight lines? Yes. Region correctly labelled? Yes.

analogy.t: The Tethered Goat and Fencing Boundaries
analogy.p: Imagine a goat tethered to a stake by a rope: the grass it can reach forms a circular locus around the stake. If you need to stay the same distance from two trees, you walk along the exact path down the middle (the perpendicular bisector), just like walking down the centre of a hallway where you are equidistant from both walls. The analogy breaks down because real goats can chew ropes and walk around obstacles, whereas mathematical loci are infinite, exact, and frictionless.

A line that divides a line segment into two equal parts at a 90-degree angle.
A line that divides an angle into two equal halves.
At an equal distance from two or more objects.
An accurate drawing of geometric figures using only a ruler and compasses.
A curved portion of a circle used in constructions.
A corner where two lines or sides meet.
The shortest distance from a point to a line, measured at 90 degrees.
An area bounded by specific loci inequalities.
A V-shaped instrument used for drawing circles and arcs.
To cut something into two equal parts.
A part of a straight line that is bounded by two distinct end points.

mistakes.w: Erasing construction arcs after finishing the drawing.
mistakes.r: Leave all construction arcs visible; examiners deduct marks if they are rubbed out.

mistakes.w: Using a protractor to measure 90 degrees for a perpendicular line.
mistakes.r: Use compass arcs to construct perpendiculars; protractors are not accepted as valid construction methods.

mistakes.w: Opening compasses to less than half the line length when constructing a perpendicular bisector.
mistakes.r: The compass radius must be greater than half the line length so the arcs intersect.

mistakes.w: Shading the wrong side of a locus inequality line.
mistakes.r: Test a point in the region (like the origin) to verify whether it satisfies the inequality before shading.

mistakes.w: Drawing freehand curves for circles or arcs.
mistakes.r: Always use a pair of compasses for any circular arc or circle.

mistakes.w: Measuring real-life distances directly without using the map scale.
mistakes.r: Convert the real-life distance using the given scale (e.g., 1 cm to 2 km) before setting your compasses.

mistakes.w: Drawing thick, blurry construction lines.
mistakes.r: Use a sharp pencil for precise intersection points.

exam.q: Construct the perpendicular bisector of the line segment AB.
model: Arcs drawn with radius greater than half AB centred at A and B
Correct straight perpendicular bisector drawn intersecting the arcs
exam.tip: Ensure your compasses stay at the same radius for both sets of arcs.

exam.q: Bisect angle XYZ using a ruler and compasses.
model: Arc drawn centred at Y cutting both arms
Intersecting arcs drawn from these points and correct bisector line drawn through Y
exam.tip: Leave all arc intersection marks visible.

exam.q: Construct a triangle with sides 7 cm, 8 cm, and 9 cm.
model: Base line of correct length drawn with a ruler
Compass arcs of correct remaining lengths drawn from each end
Triangle completed accurately with straight lines
exam.tip: Double check your compass spread against the ruler before drawing.

exam.q: A treasure is buried in a field. It is closer to tree A than tree B. Shade the possible region.
model: Perpendicular bisector of AB constructed correctly
Correct side of the bisector identified
exam.tip: Closer to A means the side containing point A.

exam.q: Find the shortest distance from point P to the straight line CD.
model: Perpendicular line constructed from P to line CD
Distance measured and stated with correct units
exam.tip: Shortest distance is always perpendicular.

exam.q: Construct the locus of points that are 4 cm from point M.
model: Compasses set accurately to 4 cm using a ruler
Complete circle drawn with centre M
exam.tip: Check your compass setting against the ruler scale.

exam.q: A boat must stay at least 3 km away from lighthouse L. Using a scale of 1 cm to 1 km, construct the forbidden region.
model: Scale conversion correctly identified as 3 cm
Circle of radius 3 cm drawn centred at L
Region inside the circle shaded as forbidden
exam.tip: At least means greater than or equal to, so shade inside the circle if it is the forbidden zone.

exam.q: Construct a 60 degree angle at point P on a straight line.
model: Arc drawn from P cutting the line
Arc of same radius drawn from intersection cutting the first arc to form 60 degrees
exam.tip: An equilateral triangle construction creates a 60 degree angle.

exam.q: A park has two paths meeting at an angle. A fountain is equidistant from both paths and 5m from the corner. Construct the possible position(s) for the fountain.
model: Angle bisector constructed between the two paths
Arc of radius 5m (using scale) drawn from the corner
exam.tip: Look for where the two different loci intersect.

worked.q: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment AB of length 8 cm.
steps: Draw a straight line AB of length 8 cm using a ruler.
Set your compasses to a radius greater than 4 cm (e.g., 5 cm).
Place the compass point on A and draw an arc above and below the line.
Without changing the radius, place the compass point on B and draw arcs to intersect the first two.
Join the two intersection points with a straight line.
worked.ans: A perpendicular bisector dividing AB into two 4 cm sections at 90 degrees, with all construction arcs visible.

worked.q: Find the shortest distance from a point P to a line AB where the scale drawing shows P is 6 cm away perpendicularly.
steps: Identify that the shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance.
Ensure the line from P meets AB at exactly 90 degrees.
Use the given map scale (e.g., 1 cm = 2 km) to convert the drawing measurement.
Calculate real distance: 6 cm x 2 km/cm = 12 km.

maths_eduqas_f.3.2.summary: This comprehensive revision guide covers all angle facts at a point, on a straight line, vertically opposite angles, and parallel line properties, alongside angle sums of triangles and polygons. You will learn to state precise geometric reasons required by examiners and solve complex multi-step angle chasing problems. Mastering these fundamental rules guarantees full marks on both non-calculator and calculator papers.

core.h: 1. Angles on a Straight Line and at a Point
core.p: Angles situated on a straight line always add up to exactly 180 degrees. Angles meeting at a full turn around a single point always sum to 360 degrees. Whenever you use these facts in an exam question, you must write down the exact geometric reason to gain full marks.
bullets: Straight line angles form a linear pair or set of supplementary angles that total 180°.
Angles around a point form a complete rotation totaling 360°.
Always write reasons: 'Angles on a straight line sum to 180°' or 'Angles at a point sum to 360°'.

callouts.p: Mark schemes allocate specific marks for stating the geometric reason. Never omit 'Angles on a straight line sum to 180°'.
Always double check your subtraction from 180 or 360, especially on non-calculator papers in Component 1.

fig.cap: Angles on a straight line summing to 180° and angles at a point summing to 360°.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><path d="M 20 120 L 220 120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="3" fill="none"/><path d="M 100 120 L 70 60" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="85" y="100" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">a</text><text x="130" y="100" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">b</text><text x="100" y="210" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">a + b = 180°</text><circle cx="310" cy="120" r="50" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="300" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">360°</text></svg>

core.p: When two straight lines intersect, they create two pairs of vertically opposite angles. Vertically opposite angles are always equal in size. This rule applies regardless of whether the intersecting lines are perpendicular or oblique.
bullets: Formed by two intersecting straight lines forming an 'X' shape.
Opposite angles across the intersection are strictly equal.
Required reason: 'Vertically opposite angles are equal'.

callouts.p: Angles that are opposite each other when two lines cross.

core.p: When a straight line called a transversal intersects a pair of parallel lines, special angle relationships are created. Identifying alternate, corresponding, and co-interior angles allows you to navigate complex multi-step geometric diagrams.
bullets: Corresponding angles are equal (forming an 'F' shape).
Alternate angles are equal (forming a 'Z' shape).
Co-interior (or allied) angles sum to 180° (forming a 'C' or 'U' shape).

callouts.p: Look out for matching arrowheads on lines; these explicitly indicate that the lines are parallel.

fig.cap: Parallel lines cut by a transversal showing corresponding and alternate angles.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="50" y1="80" x2="350" y2="80" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="50" y1="160" x2="350" y2="160" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="100" y1="40" x2="300" y2="200" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><text x="130" y="70" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">x</text><text x="190" y="150" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">x</text><text x="150" y="220" font-size="12" fill="#2563eb">Corresponding angles are equal</text></svg>

core.p: The interior angles of any triangle always add up to 180 degrees. This fundamental rule applies to acute, obtuse, right-angled, scalene, isosceles, and equilateral triangles alike.
bullets: Sum of interior angles in any triangle = 180°.
Required reason: 'Angles in a triangle sum to 180°'.
Exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.

callouts.p: An exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two interior opposite angles.

core.p: Isosceles triangles have two sides of equal length and two base angles that are equal. Equilateral triangles have three equal sides and three equal interior angles, each measuring 60 degrees.
bullets: Isosceles: Equal sides mean equal base angles. Reason: 'Base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal'.
Equilateral: All sides equal, all angles 60°. Reason: 'Angles in an equilateral triangle are 60°'.

callouts.p: Make sure you identify which angles are the base angles. They are opposite the two equal sides.

core.p: Any four-sided polygon (quadrilateral) can be split into two triangles by drawing a diagonal from one corner to the opposite corner. Since each triangle contains 180 degrees, the interior angles of any quadrilateral always sum to 360 degrees.
bullets: Sum of interior angles in any quadrilateral = 360°.
Reason: 'Angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°'.
Applies to squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapezia, kites, and irregular quadrilaterals.

core.p: To find the sum of interior angles in any polygon with n sides, divide the polygon into triangles from a single vertex, giving (n - 2) triangles. Multiply this number by 180 degrees.
bullets: Formula for sum of interior angles: Sum = (n - 2) × 180°.
Where n represents the number of sides in the polygon.

core.p: A regular polygon has sides of equal length and interior angles of equal size. Because all interior angles are equal, finding a single interior angle or exterior angle is straightforward using simple division.
bullets: Size of one interior angle in a regular n-sided polygon = ((n - 2) × 180°) / n.
Alternatively, calculate 180° minus the exterior angle.

core.p: The exterior angle of a polygon is formed by extending any side outwards. The sum of the exterior angles of any convex polygon, taken one at each vertex, is always exactly 360 degrees.
bullets: Sum of exterior angles for any polygon = 360°.
For a regular polygon with n sides, each exterior angle = 360° / n.
Interior angle + Exterior angle = 180° at any vertex.

callouts.p: Always find the exterior angle first using 360 / n when dealing with regular polygons, then subtract from 180 to find the interior angle.

fig.cap: Exterior angles of a polygon summing to 360° and interior-exterior angle pair.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><polygon points="120,60 280,60 340,160 60,160" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="180" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Interior + Exterior = 180°</text></svg>

core.p: Exam questions often combine multiple rules in a single diagram. To solve these successfully, follow a step-by-step path: identify known angles, apply parallel line or triangle rules, and systematically write down your geometric reasoning for each step.
bullets: Step 1: Scan the diagram for straight lines, parallel line arrows, or triangles.
Step 2: Calculate missing angles one by one, annotating the diagram.
Step 3: State the exact geometric reason alongside every calculation.

analogy.p: Think of parallel lines as train tracks running side by side, and a transversal track crossing them as a connecting line. Just as a train switch crosses tracks at identical angles (corresponding and alternate positions), geometric lines maintain strict proportional rules. This breaks down when tracks curve, but in Euclidean geometry, straight parallel lines never curve.

terms.d: Two angles whose sum is exactly 180 degrees.
Two angles whose sum is exactly 90 degrees.
Angles opposite each other when two straight lines intersect, which are equal.
A straight line that crosses two or more other lines.
Angles in matching corners relative to the transversal and parallel lines, which are equal (F shape).
Angles on opposite sides of the transversal between parallel lines, which are equal (Z shape).
Angles on the same side of the transversal between parallel lines, which sum to 180 degrees (C shape).
A triangle with three equal sides and three 60-degree angles.
A triangle with two equal sides and two equal base angles.
A triangle with all sides and angles of different lengths and sizes.
An angle inside a shape formed by two adjacent sides.
An angle formed outside a polygon by extending one side past a vertex.
A polygon with all sides equal in length and all interior angles equal in size.
A polygon where all interior angles are strictly less than 180 degrees.

mistakes.w: Saying angles on a straight line add up to 360°.
mistakes.r: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.

mistakes.w: Assuming co-interior angles are equal.
mistakes.r: Co-interior angles sum to 180°.

mistakes.w: Dividing by n instead of (n - 2) when finding polygon interior angle sums.
mistakes.r: Use (n - 2) × 180° for the total sum of interior angles.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to write down the geometric reason in angle proof questions.
mistakes.r: Always state the exact reason (e.g., 'Alternate angles are equal').

mistakes.w: Confusing alternate and corresponding angles.
mistakes.r: Alternate angles form a Z shape; corresponding angles form an F shape.

mistakes.w: Thinking the exterior angles of a polygon sum to 180°.
mistakes.r: Exterior angles of any polygon always sum to 360°.

exam.q: Find the size of angle x on a straight line if the adjacent angle is 65°.
model: 115° with reason 'Angles on a straight line sum to 180°'
exam.tip: Always subtract the given angle from 180 and state the reason.

exam.q: Calculate the sum of the interior angles of a regular octagon.
exam.tip: Octagon has 8 sides. Substitute n = 8 into (n - 2) × 180.

exam.q: The exterior angle of a regular polygon is 30°. How many sides does it have?
exam.tip: Number of sides = 360 divided by the exterior angle.

exam.q: Two parallel lines are intersected by a transversal. One alternate angle is given as (3x + 10)° and another is 70°. Solve for x.
exam.tip: Alternate angles are equal, so equate the two expressions.

exam.q: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 40°. Find the size of one base angle.
exam.tip: Subtract the vertex angle from 180, then divide the remaining sum equally by 2.

exam.q: Calculate the size of one interior angle of a regular decagon (10 sides).
exam.tip: Find the total interior angle sum first, then divide by the number of sides.

exam.q: In a triangle, the angles are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Find the size of the largest angle.
exam.tip: Sum the ratio parts and divide 180 by that total.

exam.q: Explain why the exterior angle and interior angle at any vertex of a polygon always sum to 180°.
model: They form a straight line together along the extended side
Angles on a straight line sum to 180°
exam.tip: Reference the straight line formed by the side and its extension.

exam.q: Find missing angle y given a quadrilateral with interior angles 85°, 110°, 95°, and y.
exam.tip: Quadrilateral interior angles sum to 360°.

worked.q: Find the size of angle x in a triangle where the other two interior angles are 52° and 68°.
steps: State the rule: Angles in a triangle sum to 180°.
Add the two known angles: 52 + 68 = 120°.
Subtract from 180°: 180 - 120 = 60°.

worked.q: A regular polygon has an interior angle of 135°. Calculate the number of sides.
steps: Find the corresponding exterior angle: 180 - 135 = 45°.
Use the exterior angle formula: n = 360 / Exterior Angle.
Calculate sides: 360 / 45 = 8 sides.

maths_eduqas_f.3.3.summary: Mastering the properties and definitions of special triangles, quadrilaterals, and other plane figures is essential for solving geometric reasoning and angle problems on both non-calculator and calculator papers. This guide covers all foundational classifications including scalene, isosceles, equilateral, and right-angled triangles, as well as kites, parallelograms, rhombuses, trapeziums, rectangles, squares, and regular polygons. Understanding sides, parallel lines, internal angle sums, and line or rotational symmetries guarantees full marks on geometric property questions.

core.h: 1. Classifying Triangles by Sides and Angles
core.p: Triangles are fundamental 2D shapes with three straight sides and internal angles summing to exactly 180 degrees. They are classified based on the relative lengths of their sides and the sizes of their internal angles.
bullets: A scalene triangle has three completely different side lengths and three different interior angle sizes.
An isosceles triangle has two equal side lengths and two equal base angles opposite those sides.
An equilateral triangle has three equal side lengths and three equal interior angles, each measuring 60 degrees.
A right-angled triangle contains one interior angle measuring exactly 90 degrees, opposite the longest side called the hypotenuse.

callouts.p: A triangle with three equal sides and three equal angles of 60 degrees.
The interior angles of any triangle always add up to 180 degrees.

fig.cap: Classification of triangles by sides and angles showing properties clearly.

core.h: 2. Properties of Quadrilaterals: Parallelogram and Rhombus
core.p: Quadrilaterals are four-sided plane figures whose interior angles sum to 360 degrees. Parallelograms and rhombuses are special quadrilaterals featuring parallel opposite sides and specific diagonal properties.
bullets: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel opposite sides and equal opposite interior angles. Consecutive angles add up to 180 degrees.
The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, meaning they cut each other exactly in half at their intersection point.
A rhombus is a special type of parallelogram where all four sides are of equal length.
The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles (90 degrees) and also bisect the interior corners.

callouts.p: Do not assume the diagonals of a standard parallelogram meet at 90 degrees; that is only true for a rhombus or square.

core.h: 3. Properties of Quadrilaterals: Trapezium and Kite
core.p: Trapeziums and kites have unique symmetry and side relationships that distinguish them from standard parallelograms and rectangles.
bullets: A trapezium has at least one pair of parallel opposite sides. An isosceles trapezium also has equal base angles and equal diagonals.
A kite has two pairs of adjacent sides that are equal in length.
The longer diagonal of a kite bisects the shorter diagonal at right angles (90 degrees).
A kite has exactly one line of symmetry passing along its main diagonal and no rotational symmetry.

callouts.p: Kite diagonals intersect at right angles, and the main diagonal splits the kite into two identical congruent triangles.

fig.cap: Properties of a kite showing perpendicular diagonals and equal adjacent sides.

core.h: 4. Rectangles and Squares: The Ultimate Quadrilaterals
core.p: Rectangles and squares are special parallelograms with additional strict angle and side constraints, forming the basis of many coordinate geometry and area problems.
bullets: A rectangle has four right angles (90 degrees) and opposite sides that are equal in parallel pairs. Its diagonals are equal in length and bisect each other.
A square is a regular quadrilateral, meaning it has four equal sides and four right angles.
A square's diagonals are equal in length, intersect at 90 degrees, and bisect the corner angles.
A square has four lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 4.

callouts.p: A quadrilateral with four equal sides and four interior right angles.

core.p: Polygons are 2D closed shapes made with straight line segments. Understanding the difference between regular and irregular polygons is vital for angle calculations.
bullets: A polygon is regular if all its sides are equal in length and all its interior angles are equal in size.
An irregular polygon has sides of varying lengths and interior angles of varying sizes.
Common named polygons include pentagon (5 sides), hexagon (6 sides), heptagon (7 sides), octagon (8 sides), nonagon (9 sides), and decagon (10 sides).
The sum of interior angles in any n-sided polygon is given by the formula 180(n - 2).

callouts.p: Always memorize standard polygon names from 3 to 10 sides to avoid losing marks in descriptive questions.

core.h: 6. Lines of Symmetry in Plane Figures
core.p: Symmetry properties describe how a shape can be folded or turned onto itself. Line symmetry (or reflection symmetry) is tested frequently in Eduqas exams.
bullets: A line of symmetry divides a 2D shape into two identical mirror-image halves.
An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of symmetry. An isosceles triangle has 1 line of symmetry. A scalene triangle has 0 lines of symmetry.
A regular pentagon has 5 lines of symmetry. A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry.
A parallelogram has 0 lines of symmetry (unless it is a rhombus or rectangle). A rhombus has 2 lines of symmetry.

callouts.p: Standard parallelograms have NO lines of symmetry, despite having parallel sides and equal opposite angles.

core.p: Rotational symmetry measures how many times a shape fits onto itself during a full 360-degree rotation around its central point.
bullets: The order of rotational symmetry is the number of times a shape maps onto itself in one complete 360-degree turn.
A circle has an infinite order of rotational symmetry.
A regular n-sided polygon has a rotational symmetry order of n.
A kite has a rotational symmetry order of 1 (meaning it only matches itself after a full 360-degree turn).

callouts.p: Shapes with an order of 1 rotational symmetry are considered to have no rotational symmetry.

core.p: A diagonal is a straight line segment joining two non-adjacent vertices of a polygon. Knowing diagonal properties helps distinguish shapes like rhombuses from rectangles.
bullets: A rectangle has two equal diagonals that bisect each other.
A rhombus has two perpendicular diagonals that bisect each other and the corner angles.
A square has two equal, perpendicular diagonals that bisect each other.
A kite has one diagonal that perpendicularly bisects the other.

callouts.p: If the diagonals of a parallelogram are equal, the shape must be a rectangle or a square.

core.h: 9. Interior and Exterior Angles of Polygons
core.p: Plane figures are defined by their boundary angles. The relationship between interior and exterior angles is a core source of marks on Foundation papers.
bullets: An interior angle is formed inside the polygon by two adjacent sides.
An exterior angle is formed by extending one side of a polygon past the vertex.
At any vertex, the interior angle plus the exterior angle always equals 180 degrees because they form a straight line.
The sum of all exterior angles in any convex polygon is always exactly 360 degrees, regardless of how many sides it has.

callouts.p: Exterior angle sum = 360 degrees for any convex polygon.

core.h: 10. Special Plane Figures: Circles and Semicircles
core.p: While polygons have straight sides, curved plane figures like circles and semicircles appear frequently in geometry and perimeter questions.
bullets: A circle is the locus of all points equidistant from a fixed centre point.
A semicircle is half of a circle, bounded by a diameter and an arc.
A quarter circle (quadrant) is bounded by two radii meeting at 90 degrees and a circular arc.
A circle has an infinite number of lines of symmetry passing through its centre and infinite rotational symmetry order.

callouts.p: Every line passing through the centre of a circle is a line of symmetry.

core.p: Exam questions often give a list of properties and ask you to name the mathematical shape. Precision in terminology is essential.
bullets: If a quadrilateral has four equal sides and diagonals that intersect at 90 degrees, it is a rhombus or a square.
If a quadrilateral has equal diagonals and four right angles, it is a rectangle or a square.
If a triangle has two equal angles, the sides opposite those angles are also equal (isosceles).
If a shape has rotational symmetry of order 2 and no lines of symmetry, it is a parallelogram.

callouts.p: If a shape could be a square or a rhombus based on the clues, state the most general correct shape unless all square properties are guaranteed.

core.p: On calculator and non-calculator papers alike, coordinate geometry is used to verify shape classifications by calculating lengths and gradients.
bullets: To prove a shape is a parallelogram, show that opposite sides have equal gradients (meaning they are parallel).
To prove perpendicular lines (such as in squares, rectangles, or kites), show that the product of their gradients is -1.
To prove side lengths are equal, use the distance formula (Pythagoras' theorem on coordinate axes).
Check midpoints of diagonals to confirm whether diagonals bisect each other.

callouts.p: Parallel lines have identical gradients. Perpendicular lines have negative reciprocal gradients.

analogy.p: Imagine shapes as members of a royal family tree where parents pass down traits to their children. A quadrilateral is the grand ancestor with four sides. A parallelogram is a child who inherited parallel opposite sides. The parallelogram then has two children: the rectangle (who inherited 90-degree corners) and the rhombus (who inherited equal side lengths). Finally, the square is the royal heir who inherited BOTH 90-degree corners and equal side lengths from both parents! This analogy breaks down when considering non-convex or complex overlapping shapes like star polygons, which do not fit neat family hierarchies.

terms.d: A triangle with three unequal sides and three different interior angles.
A triangle with two equal sides and two equal base angles.
A triangle with three equal sides and three 60-degree angles.
A quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel opposite sides.
A parallelogram with four equal sides and perpendicular diagonals.
A quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel opposite sides.
A quadrilateral with two pairs of adjacent equal sides and perpendicular diagonals.
A quadrilateral with four right angles and equal opposite sides.
A regular quadrilateral with four equal sides and four right angles.
A polygon with all sides equal in length and all interior angles equal.
An angle inside a shape formed by two adjacent sides meeting at a vertex.
An angle formed between one side of a polygon and the line extended from an adjacent side.
A straight line connecting two non-adjacent vertices of a polygon.
A property where a shape can be folded into two identical matching halves.
The number of times a shape maps onto itself during a 360-degree turn.

mistakes.w: Stating that a parallelogram has lines of symmetry.
mistakes.r: A standard parallelogram has 0 lines of symmetry; only rotation symmetry of order 2.

mistakes.w: Assuming the diagonals of a rectangle meet at 90 degrees.
mistakes.r: Rectangle diagonals are equal in length and bisect each other, but they are NOT perpendicular unless it is a square.

mistakes.w: Calling a trapezium a shape with no parallel sides.
mistakes.r: A trapezium must have at least one pair of parallel sides (by UK curriculum definition).

mistakes.w: Confusing interior and exterior angle sums for polygons.
mistakes.r: Interior angle sum is 180(n - 2); exterior angle sum is always 360 degrees.

mistakes.w: Believing an isosceles triangle can have obtuse base angles.
mistakes.r: Base angles of an isosceles triangle must be acute because two obtuse angles would exceed the 180-degree triangle sum.

mistakes.w: Writing that a kite has two lines of symmetry.
mistakes.r: A kite has exactly 1 line of symmetry (along its main diagonal).

mistakes.w: Stating a rhombus has equal diagonals.
mistakes.r: A rhombus has unequal diagonals (one long, one short) that cross at right angles.

exam.q: Write down the geometric name of a quadrilateral that has rotational symmetry of order 2 and no lines of symmetry.
exam.tip: Learn the symmetry properties of standard quadrilaterals by heart.

exam.q: A regular polygon has exterior angles of 30 degrees. How many sides does the polygon have?
exam.tip: Use the rule that the sum of exterior angles is always 360 degrees.

exam.q: Explain why a triangle with angles 70°, 70°, and 40° must be isosceles.
model: It has two equal angles (70° and 70°).
Therefore, the two sides opposite those angles must be equal in length, making it an isosceles triangle.
exam.tip: State both the angle property and the resulting side property.

exam.q: Write down the mathematical name of a 6-sided regular polygon.
exam.tip: Memorize polygon names from 3 to 10 sides.

exam.q: A quadrilateral has diagonals that are equal in length, bisect each other at right angles, and have four equal sides. What is the name of this shape?
exam.tip: Check every single property listed; equal sides + right-angle diagonals + equal diagonals strictly means a square.

exam.q: Calculate the sum of the interior angles of a regular octagon.
exam.tip: Substitute the number of sides into the formula 180(n - 2).

exam.q: State the number of lines of symmetry in a regular pentagon.
exam.tip: A regular n-sided polygon has n lines of symmetry.

exam.q: A triangle has side lengths 7 cm, 7 cm, and 10 cm. Classify this triangle.
exam.tip: Two equal sides always mean an isosceles triangle.

exam.q: Explain why a kite cannot be a parallelogram.
model: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel opposite sides.
A kite only has adjacent equal sides and does not have parallel opposite sides.
exam.tip: Compare the definitions of parallel sides in both shapes.

exam.q: Find the size of each interior angle in a regular nonagon (9 sides).
exam.tip: Find the total sum first, then divide by the number of sides.

exam.q: Two sides of a parallelogram measure 5 cm and 9 cm. What is the total perimeter of the parallelogram?
exam.tip: Remember that opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal in length.

worked.q: A regular polygon has an interior angle of 135 degrees. Calculate the number of sides of this polygon.
steps: Step 1: Find the size of the exterior angle by subtracting the interior angle from 180°. Exterior angle = 180 - 135 = 45°.
Step 2: Use the exterior angle sum formula. Since all exterior angles add up to 360° and are equal, divide 360° by the exterior angle. Number of sides n = 360 / 45.
Step 3: Calculate the final result. n = 8.

worked.q: Classify fully a quadrilateral with vertices at coordinates (1, 1), (3, 5), (7, 3), and (5, -1), showing brief gradient reasoning.
steps: Step 1: Calculate the gradients of opposite sides using change in y over change in x.
Step 2: Gradient of side 1 = (5 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 4/2 = 2. Gradient of opposite side = (-1 - 3)/(5 - 7) = -4/-2 = 2. Since gradients are equal, opposite sides are parallel.
Step 3: Check adjacent side gradients. Gradient of adjacent side = (3 - 5)/(7 - 3) = -2/4 = -0.5. Since 2 * (-0.5) = -1, the adjacent sides meet at right angles (perpendicular).
Step 4: Combine properties: equal parallel sides meeting at 90 degrees with equal diagonals.
worked.ans: Rectangle (or square, confirmed by side length calculations)

maths_eduqas_f.3.12.summary: Mastering the measurement of lines and angles, scale drawings, maps, and bearings is essential for spatial problem-solving in the Eduqas Foundation tier. You must be precise with your ruler and protractor, understand the ratio of real-world dimensions to scale models, and follow the three core rules of three-figure bearings. Careful attention to units, North lines, and clockwise direction will guarantee full marks in both non-calculator and calculator papers.

core.p: Measuring line segments requires absolute precision using a standard ruler marked in millimetres. Always align the zero mark of your ruler exactly with the starting point of the line rather than the physical edge of the plastic ruler.
bullets: Read measurements to the nearest millimetre (mm) unless specified otherwise.
Convert between centimetres and millimetres using 1 cm = 10 mm.
Ensure your eye is directly above the graduation mark to prevent parallax errors.
Check that your pencil is sharp so the line thickness does not introduce error.

callouts.p: A blunt pencil can add an extra millimetre of error. Keep your pencil needle-sharp for all geometrical drawings.
Never start measuring from the extreme left edge of the physical ruler; always start from the exact 0 cm line.

fig.cap: Correct ruler alignment showing measurement of a line segment starting strictly at the zero mark.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><rect x="50" y="80" width="300" height="50" fill="#f1f5f9" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="80" y1="105" x2="320" y2="105" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="4"/><text x="80" y="130" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">0 cm</text><text x="320" y="130" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">8 cm</text><text x="200" y="60" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#1b2540">Aligning 0 on the ruler</text></svg>

core.p: Measuring interior or exterior angles requires careful placement of the protractor centre point over the vertex of the angle and aligning the baseline precisely along one arm of the angle.
bullets: Place the crosshair or small circle of the protractor precisely on the vertex.
Align the baseline with one arm so it reads 0 degrees.
Read along the correct scale (inner or outer) depending on which side the 0 starts.
Angles smaller than 90 degrees are acute; angles between 90 and 180 degrees are obtuse.

callouts.p: The common endpoint where two line segments meet to form an angle.
Always check which scale starts at 0 on the arm you aligned. Reading the wrong scale is the number one cause of lost marks.

core.p: Scale drawings represent real-life objects or areas accurately on paper by reducing or enlarging all dimensions by the exact same ratio, known as the scale factor.
bullets: Scales are often given as ratios, such as 1 : 100 or in words like '1 cm represents 5 m'.
To find the real-life size, multiply the drawing measurement by the scale multiplier.
To find the drawing size, divide the real-life measurement by the scale multiplier.
Always keep units consistent when performing scale calculations (convert metres to centimetres).

callouts.p: Always convert your final answer into sensible real-world units (e.g. meters or kilometers) rather than leaving thousands of centimetres.

core.p: Maps use scales to show large geographical areas on a small sheet of paper. Map scales can be expressed as a ratio statement or shown visually using a linear bar scale.
bullets: Linear bar scales remain accurate even if a map is photocopied or resized digitally.
Convert map distances to real distances using the given ratio multiplier.
Remember that 1 kilometre equals 100,000 centimetres (1 km = 1000 m = 100,000 cm).
Measure the straight-line distance on the map with a ruler before applying the scale.

callouts.p: If a map is scanned or resized in an exam, use the printed bar scale rather than a written ratio because the bar scale scales with the image.

core.p: Bearings are a standardized way of describing direction using angles. They are vital for navigation, hiking, and sailing.
bullets: Bearings are always measured from North.
Bearings are always measured in a clockwise direction.
Bearings are always written using exactly three figures (e.g., 045 degrees or 270 degrees).
A full turn around a point is 360 degrees.

callouts.p: A three-figure angle measured clockwise from the North line.
Writing 45 degrees instead of 045 degrees will lose you a mark. Bearings must always have three digits.

fig.cap: Standard compass directions with their corresponding three-figure bearings measured clockwise from North.

core.p: To measure the bearing of point B from point A, you must draw a North line at point A, connect A to B with a straight line, and measure the clockwise angle.
bullets: Locate the 'from' point (point A); draw a vertical North arrow pointing straight up from it.
Draw a straight line connecting point A to point B.
Place your protractor centre at point A with 0 aligned with the North line.
Read the clockwise angle round to the line AB.

callouts.p: The North line is always drawn at the point where the word 'from' originates. If asked for the bearing of B *from* A, draw North at A.

core.p: When given a starting point, a bearing, and a distance, you must construct the position of a second point accurately using a protractor and a ruler.
bullets: Mark the starting point and draw a clear North line pointing straight up.
Use your protractor to measure the given clockwise angle from North and make a small pencil mark.
Draw a straight line from the starting point through your pencil mark.
Measure the exact required distance along this line using your ruler and mark the final point.

callouts.p: Draw your construction ray very lightly so it can be easily erased if adjustments are needed.

core.p: If you know the bearing of B from A, you can easily calculate the bearing of A from B (the return bearing) without measuring again, using parallel line angle rules.
bullets: If the original bearing is less than 180 degrees, add 180 degrees to find the back bearing.
If the original bearing is greater than 180 degrees, subtract 180 degrees to find the back bearing.
North lines at different points are parallel, so co-interior (alli-interior) angles sum to 180 degrees.
Always check your calculation makes logical sense on a sketch.

callouts.p: Back bearings always differ from forward bearings by exactly 180 degrees. Add 180 if under 180, subtract 180 if over 180.
A back bearing of 30 degrees must still be written as 030 degrees.

core.h: Solving Multi-Step Scale and Bearing Problems
core.p: Examination questions often combine scale drawings, bearings, and basic trigonometry or Pythagoras in context, testing your ability to follow structured instructions.
bullets: Read the entire question carefully before starting your construction or calculation.
Check that your scale conversion factor is applied correctly to every measured length.
Label all intermediate points clearly with capital letters.
Double-check your protractor alignment if your final answer differs from the expected tolerance range.

callouts.p: Examiners allow a small tolerance (usually plus or minus 2 degrees for angles and plus or minus 2 millimetres for lengths) in construction questions.

analogy.p: Imagine you are hiking through dense woodland with a topographic map and a magnetic compass. The map uses a scale where every centimeter on paper represents one hundred meters of rugged terrain, meaning a tiny finger-span on paper translates to a long trek in reality. When you stand at a checkpoint, your compass orientates you to true North so you can measure your exact three-figure bearing before setting off in a straight line. Where this analogy breaks down is that real terrain has hills, valleys, and winding paths, whereas map distances and bearings deal exclusively with flat, straight-line displacement.

terms.d: A direction measured as an angle in degrees, strictly clockwise from the North line, expressed in three figures.
A drawing that represents an object or place accurately using a fixed ratio to enlarge or reduce dimensions.
The multiplier used to scale all dimensions between a model/drawing and real life.
A reference line pointing directly towards magnetic or true North, used as the starting baseline for measuring bearings.
The return bearing from the destination back to the starting point, differing by exactly 180 degrees.
The point where two line segments or rays meet to form an angle.
An angle measuring strictly between 0 and 90 degrees.
An angle measuring strictly between 90 and 180 degrees.
A graphical line divided into sections representing specific real-life units on a map or drawing.
An error in reading an instrument caused by the observer's eye not being perpendicular to the scale mark.
A bearing format requiring leading zeros where necessary, such as 045 degrees instead of 45 degrees.
A semi-circular or circular instrument marked in degrees used for measuring and drawing angles.

mistakes.w: Writing a bearing as 45 degrees instead of 045 degrees.
mistakes.r: Bearings must always be written with exactly three figures; add a leading zero.

mistakes.w: Measuring bearings anti-clockwise from North.
mistakes.r: Bearings must always be measured in a clockwise direction from the North line.

mistakes.w: Starting measurements from the edge of the ruler rather than the 0 cm mark.
mistakes.r: Align the 0 mark of the ruler precisely with the start of the line.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert units when using map scales (e.g., using cm directly as km).
mistakes.r: Always convert map centimeters to real-world meters or kilometers using the correct conversion factor.

mistakes.w: Drawing the North line at the wrong point in bearing questions.
mistakes.r: Always draw the North line at the 'from' point where the bearing measurement originates.

mistakes.w: Adding 180 degrees to a back bearing that is already greater than 180 degrees.
mistakes.r: If the original bearing is greater than 180 degrees, subtract 180 degrees to find the back bearing.

mistakes.w: Reading the wrong scale (inner vs outer) on the protractor.
mistakes.r: Check which scale starts at 0 degrees along the aligned arm of your angle.

exam.q: Measure the length of the line segment AB in centimeters.
model: Correct measurement within tolerance of 6.2 cm to 6.4 cm.
exam.tip: Ensure your ruler's zero mark is precisely at point A.

exam.q: Write down the three-figure bearing of East.
exam.tip: Remember all bearings require three digits.

exam.q: The scale of a map is 1 cm represents 4 km. The distance between two towns on the map is 3.5 cm. Find the actual distance in kilometers.
exam.tip: Multiply the map distance by the scale value.

exam.q: The bearing of ship B from ship A is 055°. Calculate the bearing of ship A from ship B.
exam.tip: Since the angle is less than 180 degrees, add 180 degrees.

exam.q: A scale drawing has a ratio of 1 : 250. A garden fence is represented by a line of length 12 cm on the drawing. Calculate the actual length of the fence in meters.
exam.tip: Convert centimetres to metres at the end by dividing by 100.

exam.q: The bearing of town X from town Y is 240°. Calculate the bearing of town Y from town X.
exam.tip: Since the angle is greater than 180 degrees, subtract 180 degrees and format as 060.

exam.q: On a map with a scale of 1 cm : 500 m, the distance between two landmarks is 2.5 cm. Work out the actual distance in kilometers.
exam.tip: Convert meters to kilometers by dividing by 1000.

exam.q: Measure the obtuse angle ABC using a protractor.
model: Correct protractor alignment at vertex B
exam.tip: Make sure you read the obtuse scale (>90 degrees).

exam.q: A plane flies from airfield P on a bearing of 072° for a distance represented by 8 cm on a scale of 1 cm to 50 km. Calculate the actual distance flown.
exam.tip: Ignore the bearing when calculating the distance; just multiply drawing length by scale.

exam.q: Explain why a bearing can never be 410°.
model: A full turn is only 360 degrees, so bearings cannot exceed 360°.
exam.tip: Relate your answer to the maximum angle in a full circle.

worked.q: A map has a scale of 1 cm : 25 km. Two cities are 7.2 cm apart on the map. Find their actual distance apart in kilometers.
steps: Identify the scale factor: 1 cm represents 25 km.
Multiply the map distance by the scale factor: 7.2 x 25.
Calculate the result: 180 km.

worked.q: The bearing of point A from point B is 135°. Work out the bearing of point B from point A.
steps: Identify that this is a back bearing calculation.
Since the original bearing (135°) is less than 180°, add 180°.
Calculation: 135 + 180 = 315°.

maths_eduqas_f.3.14.summary: Mastering the geometry of circles and 3D solids is essential for securing top marks in Eduqas GCSE Mathematics. This guide covers calculating the circumference and area of circles, as well as the surface area and volume of spheres, pyramids, cones, and composite solids. You will learn to use formulae correctly, handle pi accurately, and break down complex shapes into simpler components.

core.p: The perimeter of a circle is called the circumference. The distance across the circle passing through the centre is the diameter, while the distance from the centre to any point on the edge is the radius. You must memorize and apply the exact formulae for circumference and area in both calculator and non-calculator settings.
bullets: Circumference formula: C = pi * d or C = 2 * pi * r
Area formula: A = pi * r^2
Radius is always half of the diameter (r = d / 2)
Always check whether the question asks for an exact answer in terms of pi or a rounded decimal

callouts.p: The linear distance around the outer boundary of a circle.
Always use the calculator's pi button rather than 3.14 or 22/7 unless explicitly told otherwise.

core.p: A sphere is a perfectly round three-dimensional geometrical object. The surface area of a sphere represents the total area of its outer curved surface. The formula is directly tied to the square of its radius.
bullets: Surface area formula: SA = 4 * pi * r^2
Make sure you identify the radius, not the diameter, before substituting into the formula
Units for surface area are always squared (e.g., cm^2)
Remember that 4 * pi * r^2 is four times the area of a flat circle with the same radius

callouts.p: A common mistake is using the diameter instead of the radius in the surface area formula.

core.p: The volume of a sphere measures the three-dimensional space enclosed within its curved boundary. Foundation tier questions will provide the necessary formula or test your ability to substitute values correctly.
bullets: Volume formula: V = (4/3) * pi * r^3
Note the power of 3 because volume is cubic units
Be careful with calculator bracket placement when cubing the radius
Check rounding instructions carefully (e.g., to 1 decimal place or 3 significant figures)

callouts.p: When calculating, enter (4 / 3) * pi * r^3 carefully to avoid order of operations errors.

core.p: A pyramid is a 3D shape with a flat polygonal base and triangular faces that meet at a common point called the apex. To find the total surface area, calculate the area of the base and add the areas of all the triangular faces.
bullets: Total surface area = Area of base + Area of all lateral triangular faces
For a square-based pyramid, there is 1 square base and 4 identical triangles
Remember that the height of the triangular face is the slant height, not the vertical height
Draw a net if you are struggling to visualise all the individual faces

callouts.p: Always use Pythagoras' theorem to find the slant height if only the vertical height and base dimensions are given.

core.p: The volume of any pyramid is found by taking one-third of the area of its base multiplied by its perpendicular height. This relationship holds true for square, rectangular, and triangular-based pyramids.
bullets: Volume formula: V = (1/3) * Base Area * Height
Height must be the perpendicular (vertical) height, not the slant height
For a square-based pyramid, Base Area = base length squared
Always include cubic units for volume answers

callouts.p: The shortest vertical distance from the apex straight down to the base at a 90-degree angle.

core.p: A cone has a circular base and a smooth curved surface tapering towards a top point called the apex. The total surface area is the sum of the curved surface area and the circular base area.
bullets: Curved surface area formula: CSA = pi * r * l (where l is the slant height)
Total surface area formula: TSA = pi * r * l + pi * r^2
The slant height (l) runs along the outside of the cone from the base edge to the apex
If slant height is missing, use Pythagoras' theorem with radius and vertical height

callouts.p: Never use the vertical height in the cone surface area formula; you must use the slant height (l).

fig.cap: A cone showing radius (r), vertical height (h), and slant height (l).

core.p: The volume of a cone is precisely one-third of the volume of a cylinder with the same base radius and height. This means three cones of water would fill a cylinder of identical dimensions.
bullets: Volume formula: V = (1/3) * pi * r^2 * h
Here, h represents the vertical height, not the slant height
Substitute the radius and height directly into the formula
Ensure your final answer has correct units (e.g., cm^3)

callouts.p: A cone's volume is exactly 1/3 of a cylinder's volume with matching radius and height.

core.p: Composite solids are made by joining two or more standard 3D shapes together, such as a cylinder topped with a hemisphere or a cone on top of a cylinder. To find total volumes, calculate the volume of each individual part and add them together.
bullets: Break the composite shape down into familiar standard shapes
Calculate the volume or surface area of each part separately
Add volumes together for total volume
For surface area, be careful: shared internal faces where shapes touch must NOT be included in the total surface area

callouts.p: Do not count surfaces that are hidden where two shapes are glued together when calculating total surface area.

core.p: Sometimes a composite solid has a cavity or part removed from it, such as a solid cylinder with a smaller cylindrical hole drilled through the middle. In these cases, you subtract the volume of the removed part from the main body.
bullets: Identify the outer main shape and the inner removed shape
Calculate the volume of the outer shape
Calculate the volume of the inner cavity
Subtract the inner volume from the outer volume to find the remaining volume

callouts.p: Always show your working for each individual shape so examiners can award method marks even if your final arithmetic has a slip.

analogy.p: Calculating properties of composite solids is just like building with Lego. To find out how much plastic a complex model uses (volume), you calculate the pieces separately and add them up. However, if you are painting the model (surface area), you must remember that where two bricks snap together, those touching faces are hidden and do not get painted! This breaks down slightly when dealing with curved contact patches like a hemisphere on a cylinder, where exact overlapping areas require careful subtraction.

terms.d: The distance all the way around the outer boundary of a circle.
A straight line from the centre of a circle to any point on its circumference.
A straight line passing completely through the centre of a circle, connecting two points on its circumference.
The mathematical constant representing the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, approximately 3.14159.
The total area of all the outer faces and surfaces of a three-dimensional object.
The amount of three-dimensional space enclosed by a closed surface, measured in cubic units.
A three-dimensional geometrical object shaped like a perfectly round ball.
A 3D shape with a polygonal base and triangular lateral faces meeting at a single apex.
A 3D solid with a circular base and a smooth curved surface tapering to a point.
The length measured along the lateral surface of a cone or pyramid from the base edge to the apex.
The vertical height measured at right angles from the base to the highest point or apex.
A geometric shape formed by combining two or more standard 3D shapes.

mistakes.w: Using the diameter instead of the radius in circle area or sphere volume formulae
mistakes.r: Always divide the diameter by 2 first to find the radius before calculating.

mistakes.w: Using the vertical height instead of the slant height in cone surface area
mistakes.r: Use slant height (l) for curved surface area of cones, and vertical height (h) for volume.

mistakes.w: Including hidden touching faces when calculating composite surface area
mistakes.r: Only calculate and sum the exposed outer surfaces of the combined shape.

mistakes.w: Forgetting that a sphere volume formula contains a cubed radius and 4/3 factor
mistakes.r: Learn V = (4/3)*pi*r^3 exactly and check bracket usage on your calculator.

mistakes.w: Writing square units for volume and cubic units for area
mistakes.r: Remember: length is cm, area is cm^2, volume is cm^3.

mistakes.w: Leaving out pi in the final answer when not required
mistakes.r: Unless an exact answer in terms of pi is requested, convert your answer to a decimal.

exam.q: Calculate the circumference of a circle with a diameter of 14 cm. Use pi = 3.14.
exam.tip: Check whether the question specifies a value for pi or requires the calculator button.

exam.q: Find the area of a circle with a radius of 6 cm. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
exam.tip: Square the radius first before multiplying by pi.

exam.q: Calculate the volume of a sphere with a radius of 5 cm. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
exam.tip: Use the fraction button on your calculator for 4/3 to maintain full accuracy.

exam.q: A square-based pyramid has a base side length of 6 cm and a perpendicular height of 10 cm. Calculate its volume.
exam.tip: Remember the 1/3 multiplier for pyramids and cones.

exam.q: Calculate the curved surface area of a cone with radius 4 cm and slant height 9 cm. Give your answer in terms of pi.
exam.tip: Read carefully: 'in terms of pi' means leave pi in your final answer.

exam.q: A solid cylinder has a radius of 3 cm and a height of 10 cm. Calculate its total surface area to 1 decimal place.
exam.tip: Break the cylinder into two circular ends and one rectangular curved sheet when rolled out.

exam.q: A composite solid is made from a hemisphere of radius 3 cm sitting on top of a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 8 cm. Calculate the total volume of the solid to 1 decimal place.
exam.tip: Remember a hemisphere is half of a sphere, so multiply sphere volume by 0.5.

exam.q: The circumference of a circular pond is 31.4 metres. Calculate the radius of the pond. Use pi = 3.14.
exam.tip: Rearrange the formula before substituting values if you find it easier to solve.

exam.q: Find the surface area of a sphere with a diameter of 12 cm. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
exam.tip: Always check whether the question gives you the radius or the diameter.

worked.q: Calculate the total surface area of a solid cone with a base radius of 5 cm and a vertical height of 12 cm. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
steps: Find the slant height (l) using Pythagoras' theorem: l^2 = r^2 + h^2
l = sqrt(169) = 13 cm
Calculate base area: pi * r^2 = pi * 5^2 = 25pi
Calculate curved surface area: pi * r * l = pi * 5 * 13 = 65pi
Total surface area = 25pi + 65pi = 90pi = 282.743...
Round to 1 decimal place: 282.7 cm^2

worked.q: A solid metal shape consists of a cylinder with a cone attached to one end. The cylinder and cone both have a radius of 4 cm. The cylinder has a height of 10 cm, and the cone has a slant height of 7 cm. Calculate the total surface area of this composite solid. Use pi = 3.14159.
steps: Identify exposed surfaces: Cylinder curved area, Cylinder bottom base, Cone curved area
Cylinder curved area = 2 * pi * r * h = 2 * pi * 4 * 10 = 80pi
Cylinder bottom base area = pi * r^2 = pi * 4^2 = 16pi
Cone curved area = pi * r * l = pi * 4 * 7 = 28pi
Note: The touching circular face between cone and cylinder is internal and NOT included
Total surface area = 80pi + 16pi + 28pi = 124pi
Round to 1 decimal place: 389.6 cm^2

maths_eduqas_f.3.8.summary: Mastering coordinate geometry at Foundation tier involves plotting points, identifying coordinates, and applying standard formulas to solve geometrical problems. You must be confident working with horizontal and vertical lines, calculating the midpoint of a line segment, and finding the length of a line using Pythagoras' theorem. These revision notes provide a complete guide to all coordinate geometry topics required for Eduqas Components 1 and 2.

core.p: The Cartesian coordinate system uses two perpendicular number lines, called the x-axis (horizontal) and the y-axis (vertical), intersecting at the origin (0, 0). Every point on the plane is identified by an ordered pair of numbers written as (x, y).
bullets: The x-coordinate is always written first, followed by the y-coordinate.
The origin has coordinates (0, 0).
The four quadrants divide the plane based on the signs of x and y.
Quadrant 1: (+, +), Quadrant 2: (-, +), Quadrant 3: (-, -), Quadrant 4: (+, -).

callouts.p: A pair of numbers (x, y) that specifies the precise location of a point on a coordinate grid.
Always move along the corridor (x-axis) before going up or down the stairs (y-axis). Writing (y, x) will lose all marks.

core.p: Special lines on a coordinate grid have very simple equations because every point on the line shares a common coordinate.
bullets: A horizontal line has the equation y = c, where c is a constant.
Every point on the line y = 3 has a y-coordinate of 3, such as (1, 3), (-4, 3), and (5, 3).
A vertical line has the equation x = k, where k is a constant.
Every point on the line x = -2 has an x-coordinate of -2, such as (-2, 1), (-2, 5), and (-2, -4).
The x-axis is the horizontal line with the equation y = 0.
The y-axis is the vertical line with the equation x = 0.

callouts.p: y = number is always horizontal. x = number is always vertical. Do not mix them up!

core.p: The midpoint is the exact halfway point between two given points on a coordinate grid. You calculate it by finding the mean (average) of the x-coordinates and the mean of the y-coordinates.
bullets: Formula for midpoint M: M = ((x1 + x2) / 2, (y1 + y2) / 2).
Add the two x-coordinates together and divide by 2.
Add the two y-coordinates together and divide by 2.
Write your final answer as coordinate pairs inside brackets.

callouts.p: Midpoint = (Average of x, Average of y) = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)
The midpoint must lie directly on the straight line connecting the two points. Sketching a quick mental picture helps verify this.

core.p: To find the shortest distance between two points on a coordinate grid, you use Pythagoras' theorem. The horizontal and vertical distances form a right-angled triangle.
bullets: Find the horizontal change: a = x2 - x1.
Find the vertical change: b = y2 - y1.
Square both changes: a squared and b squared.
Add the squared values together: a squared + b squared.
Take the square root of the sum to find the length: distance = square root of (a squared + b squared).

callouts.p: Distance = square root of ((x2 - x1) squared + (y2 - y1) squared)

core.p: You may be given three vertices of a shape (such as a rectangle, parallelogram, or kite) and asked to find the missing fourth vertex.
bullets: Plot the given points carefully on the provided grid.
Use properties of shapes: opposite sides of a rectangle or parallelogram are equal in length and parallel.
Count grid squares horizontally and vertically from vertex to vertex.
Check your completed shape by ensuring all required geometric properties hold true.

callouts.p: For shapes on axes, use coordinate differences and grid counting instead of complex formulas when finding missing vertices.

core.h: 6. Equations of Straight Lines (y = mx + c)
core.p: Every straight line can be written in the form y = mx + c. Understanding what m and c represent is vital for solving graphical problems.
bullets: m represents the gradient (steepness) of the line.
c represents the y-intercept (where the line crosses the vertical y-axis).
A positive gradient slopes upwards from left to right.
A negative gradient slopes downwards from left to right.

callouts.p: Gradient m = Change in y / Change in x = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)

core.h: 7. Finding the Equation of a Line
core.p: Given a graph or two points, you can determine the full equation of a straight line by finding its gradient and y-intercept.
bullets: Step 1: Calculate the gradient m using two points on the line.
Step 2: Substitute m and a known point (x, y) into y = mx + c to solve for c.
Step 3: Write out the final equation with your values of m and c.

callouts.p: Never leave c as an unknown letter in your final equation. You must calculate its numerical value.

core.p: Parallel lines are straight lines that never meet. In coordinate geometry, parallel lines share a very special property regarding their gradients.
bullets: Parallel lines always have identical gradients.
If line A has equation y = 3x + 1, any line parallel to it will start with y = 3x.
To find a parallel line passing through a given point, use the same gradient m and substitute the point to find c.

callouts.p: If two lines are parallel, m1 = m2.

core.p: Inequalities on coordinate axes define regions rather than single lines. You must know how to represent these regions shading or unshaded as instructed.
bullets: Strict inequalities (< or >) use dashed boundary lines.
Inclusive inequalities (<= or >=) use solid boundary lines.
Test a coordinate point (like 0, 0) to determine which side of the line to shade.

callouts.p: Always test (0, 0) if it does not lie on the line. It makes arithmetic extremely simple.

core.p: Coordinate axes are frequently used to display real-life relationships, such as currency conversion, temperature scales, or distance-time relationships.
bullets: Identify the scale on each axis carefully before reading values.
Draw construction lines from the axis to the graph line to read intermediate values accurately.
Interpret the gradient as a rate of change (e.g., miles per hour or pounds per euro).

callouts.p: Always check what each small square represents on both axes before attempting to read off coordinates.

analogy.t: Finding coordinates and midpoints is like reading a city map and finding the meeting point of two friends.
analogy.p: Imagine a city where streets are laid out in a grid of numbered avenues and streets. Your home is at (2, 3) and your friend's home is at (6, 5). To find where you both should meet halfway, you take the average of your avenue numbers and the average of your street numbers. This gives you the exact midpoint address! Where this analogy breaks down is that real cities have rivers, one-way systems, and diagonal roads, whereas mathematical coordinate planes are perfectly flat, infinite, and follow strict linear rules.

terms.d: A grid system defined by a horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis intersecting at right angles at the origin.
The fixed reference point (0, 0) where the x-axis and y-axis intersect.
A pair of numbers (x, y) giving the exact location of a point.
The point exactly halfway between two given endpoints.
A measure of the steepness of a straight line, calculated as change in y divided by change in x.
The point where a graph crosses the vertical y-axis, given by the value c in y = mx + c.
Straight lines that are always equidistant and never intersect, sharing the exact same gradient.
A flat straight line parallel to the x-axis, with the equation y = c.
An upright straight line parallel to the y-axis, with the equation x = k.
A finite part of a straight line defined by two distinct endpoints.
The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
The four regions into which the coordinate plane is divided by the x-axis and y-axis.

mistakes.w: Writing coordinates as (y, x) instead of (x, y).
mistakes.r: Always write the x-coordinate first, followed by the y-coordinate.

mistakes.w: Subtracting coordinates instead of adding them when finding a midpoint.
mistakes.r: Find the mean of the coordinates: add them together and divide by 2.

mistakes.w: Confusing equations of horizontal and vertical lines (e.g. thinking x = 4 is horizontal).
mistakes.r: Remember: y = c is horizontal, x = k is vertical.

mistakes.w: Calculating gradient as change in x divided by change in y.
mistakes.r: Gradient is vertical change divided by horizontal change (Rise over Run: change in y / change in x).

mistakes.w: Forgetting to square root when calculating the length of a line segment using Pythagoras.
mistakes.r: Remember that a squared + b squared = c squared, so you must take the square root at the end.

mistakes.w: Assuming perpendicular lines have the same gradient.
mistakes.r: Only parallel lines have the same gradient. Perpendicular gradients are negative reciprocals (Higher tier).

mistakes.w: Leaving the y-intercept c out of a linear equation.
mistakes.r: A complete linear equation must include both the gradient m and intercept c in the form y = mx + c.

exam.q: Write down the coordinates of the midpoint of the line segment joining (2, 3) and (8, 7).
exam.tip: Add the x values and halve them, then add the y values and halve them.

exam.q: Find the length of the line segment joining the points (1, 2) and (4, 6).
exam.tip: This forms a classic 3-4-5 right-angled triangle.

exam.q: A line has the equation y = 4x - 5. Write down the gradient of this line.
model: Identify m from y = mx + c
exam.tip: The gradient is always the coefficient of x when the equation is in the form y = mx + c.

exam.q: A line passes through the point (0, 3) and has a gradient of 2. Write down its equation.
model: Identify y-intercept c = 3 from the point (0, 3)
exam.tip: Any point in the form (0, c) gives you the y-intercept directly.

exam.q: Find the equation of the line that passes through (1, 5) and is parallel to y = 3x + 2.
model: State that parallel lines have the same gradient, so m = 3
Substitute m = 3 and point (1, 5) into y = 3x + c: 5 = 3(1) + c
exam.tip: Parallel lines share the exact same m value.

exam.q: The points A(1, 2), B(5, 2), and C(5, 6) are three vertices of a rectangle. Find the coordinates of vertex D.
model: Identify the x-coordinate of D from vertex A: x = 1
Identify the y-coordinate of D from vertex C: y = 6
exam.tip: Sketch the points on rough paper to visualize the rectangle.

exam.q: Write down the equation of the horizontal line that passes through the point (-3, 7).
model: Horizontal lines are of the form y = c
exam.tip: For a horizontal line, every y-coordinate is identical.

exam.q: Write down the equation of the vertical line that passes through the point (4, -2).
model: Vertical lines are of the form x = k
exam.tip: For a vertical line, every x-coordinate is identical.

exam.q: Calculate the gradient of the line passing through (2, 3) and (6, 11).
exam.tip: Use the gradient formula: (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1).

exam.q: Determine if the point (3, 13) lies on the line y = 4x + 1. You must show working.
model: Conclusion: Since 13 matches the y-coordinate, the point lies on the line.
exam.tip: Substitute the x-coordinate into the expression and check if it equals the y-coordinate.

worked.q: Find the midpoint and the length of the line segment joining P(2, 1) and Q(6, 4).
steps: Step 1: Calculate the midpoint using M = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2).
Step 2: Midpoint x = (2 + 6)/2 = 8/2 = 4.
Step 3: Midpoint y = (1 + 4)/2 = 5/2 = 2.5.
Step 4: Calculate length using Pythagoras. Horizontal change = 6 - 2 = 4. Vertical change = 4 - 1 = 3.
Step 5: Length = square root of (4 squared + 3 squared) = square root of (16 + 9) = square root of 25 = 5.
worked.ans: Midpoint is (4, 2.5) and Length is 5 units.

worked.q: Find the equation of the straight line passing through the points (2, 7) and (4, 13) in the form y = mx + c.
steps: Step 1: Find the gradient m using (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1).
Step 3: Substitute m = 3 and point (2, 7) into y = 3x + c.
Step 5: Write the final equation.
